BEREZOV, a town of Siberia, on the river Soswa, 18 m. from its confluence with the Obi, 420 m. N of Tobolsk, in N lat. 64°. B. provides Tobolsk, and other places on the Irtish, with dried fish in summer, and frozen fish during winter. It has also an active trade in furs. This is the most northern place in Siberia in which the horse can exist in health and vigour. Beyond B. the reindeer becomes the substitute for the horse. The ground freezes to the depth of 5 ft., yet barley and rye are cultivated with success. It was here that the three favourites of Peter the Great, Osterman, Dolgorukof, and Menschikof, ended their days in exile.

BESHKOLSKOI, a long saline lake, or rather a series of saline lakes and pools and sedgy marshes, in the Russian gov. of Astrakan, on the road from Astrakan to Glubokinskoi. These lakes appear to have originated in an inlet of the Caspian sea, which has become gradually choked by drift-sand.—Pallas.

BESHTAU, a calcareous ridge of mountains in S Russia, forming the most northern spur of the Caucasus. It runs between the valleys of the Kuma and the Kuban; and rises progressively towards the SW. On the N and E an extensive plain presents itself. Its principal summit—which is generally known as the B. par excellence—appears to rise from a kind of table-land greatly elevated above the level of the Kuma and the Podkuma. It is a mass of ancient limestone, presenting few fossils. From near its summit several narrow ridges run off towards the four adjacent mountains; whence the name Beshtau, or 'the Five Mounts.' Pallas gives a full notice of the botany of this region.

BESLINIANS, or BESSLINIZI, a tribe in the western part of Circassia, who, according to a recent Russian account, numbered 17,000 families in 1804. They reside beyond the Kuban, on the Upper Laba, at its exit from the high mountains, and extend themselves as far as the Khots, and to the source of the Psefir. where it touches on the Moukhoch or Mashokhi. The chiefs of this tribe are the ancestors of those of the Kabardali. The Beslinians join with the Kabardinians and Nogays, established on the Russian territory, in their forays. They are rich in cattle, especially in sheep. In winter they keep their cattle near their dwellings on the Laba, in enclosures of hurdles. In spring and autumn they graze them on the banks of the Urup, the Great Injek, and the salt lake of Kasma.

BESRODNAYA SLOBODA, or VERKNEI AKHTUBINSKOI GORODOK, a village of Asiatic Russia, between the rivers Volga and Akhtuba, in the vicinity of the Caspian. The empress Elizabeth established a settlement here for the culture of silk, and sent Armenians and other foreigners to assist its progress. Catherine II., following up the designs of her predecessor, prepared instructions under her own hand to promote this object, and 1,300 families were brought to the banks of the Akhtuba, where they were located in six villages, with certain immunities. Though these exertions were attended with partial success, the cultivators testified an invincible dislike to their occupation, and the quantity of silk declined yearly under their reluctant labours: at last they contrived secretly to destroy the worms by sprinkling them with salt, and to set fire to the grass around the mulberry-trees. The government in consequence ordered the culture of silk at B. to be abandoned.

BIALYSTOCK, a province of Western Russia, which formerly constituted a part of the Polish waivodeship of Podlachia, but was incorporated with Russia in 1795. In 1807, a large portion of it was incorporated with the duchy of Warsaw, in terms of the treaty of Tilsit; and the remainder was erected into the prov. we are now to describe, which was placed under the superintendence of the governors-general of Grodno, and divided into 4 districts, named from the principal towns, Bialystock, Sokolka, Bielsk, and Drohiczyn. Its superficial extent has been estimated by Wiehmann, in 1813, at 158 German or 3,355 English sq. m.; and by Broemsen, in 1819, at 169 German or 3,589 English sq. m. The pop. in 1839 amounted to 227,106, of whom 31,376 were Jews. The greater part of this pop. are Catholics, of Polish-Mazovian descent. The surface is generally flat; and the soil light and sandy. Upwards of a seventh part of the surface is covered with forests. The principal river is the Western Bug. Its tributaries, the Nurzek and the Narawa, are considerable streams. The climate is temperate; but the great extent of marshy ground renders it, in many parts, unhealthy. Rye, wheat, buck-wheat, and flax are extensively grown; and the number of individuals engaged in agriculture was returned in 1830 at 198,502, or nearly five-sixths of the whole pop. …

txt: COSSACKS, or Kozaks, a military nation inhabiting the SW frontiers of the Russian empire, bordering on Turkey, Poland, Tartary, Siberia, and the Caucasian Isthmus; and constituting the principal defence against hostile incursions from these quarters. The origin of this people has never been satisfactorily ascertained. Some regard them as an offshoot of the great Slavonic stock; others are of opinion that they originally migrated from the Caucasian isthmus, and that they chiefly belong to the Tcherkess or Circassian nations. Others suppose them to have descended from the inhabitants of Casachia, a district lying between the sea of Azof and the Caspian, mentioned by Constantine Porphyrogenitus, a writer of the 9th cent. But, asks M. Hommaire de Hell, "is there any probability that the people of Casachia, after 600 years of absolute obscurity, and whose territory lay directly in the route of all those conquering hordes that, issuing from Asia, overran and ravaged Europe, and disappeared successively, should have again arisen out of the chaos of all these revolutions to produce the C. of our day? We have ourselves traversed those Russian deserts, up to the northern foot of the Caucasus; and except the somewhat modern remains of Madjar, on the borders of the Kuma, we nowhere found any vestige of human occupancy, or any trace of civilization. …

txt: BORODINO, a village of Russia in Europe, in the gov. and 70 m. WSW of Moscow, in the dist. and 10 m. W of Mojaisk, on the Kologa, a small affluent of the Moskva. It is celebrated as the scene of a great battle between the Russians and the French on 7th September, 1812. The Russians having collected a force of about 120,000 men, determined to risk a general engagement on this spot, less in the hope of decisive success, than on the calculation of obliging the French to pay dearly for their ground, and weakening them against the approach of winter. On the right of the Russians was the river Moskwa; on their left a thick coppice of underwood, with a battery; the length of their line was about 4 m, protected at intervals by batteries, particularly towards the right. Their position was not particularly strong, the country being flat; but their artillery was ample. Aware that the left was his vulnerable point, Kutusoff, who commanded the Russians, threw up a redoubt about half-a-mile in its front; but the French van got possession of it two days before the battle. Bonaparte reconnoitred the whole position on the 6th, and determined to make his chief attack on the Russian left. On the 7th both armies were drawn up by sun-rise, and the batteries of several hundred field-pieces on each side, opened at 6 o'clock. No sweeping manœuvres took place on this first day. …

BUCHTARMINSK, a town of Asiatic Russia, in the gov. of Tomsk, at the mouth of the Buchtarma, and on the r. bank of the Irtish, which is here 374 ft. above the level of Ust-Kamenogorsk. Pop. 800. It is about 100 versts from the Chinese outposts near Narym, on the N side of the Saisang lake.
BUDENITSCHI, a town of Russia, in the gov. of Minsk, SW of Bobrinsk.

BUI, a town of Russia, in the gov. of Kostroma, at the influx of the Wocksa into the Kostroma. Pop. 1,200. BUI, Boidi, or Boion, a rocky islet in the Grecian archipelago, NW of Paros, in N lat. 37° 10'.- Also an islet on the coast of Serpho, about 2 m. to the E of the port. It is sometimes called Poloni.
BUIKO'VA, a village of Russia, in the gov. of Perm, 41 versts NW of Bisersk, in a level and fertile country, at about 580 ft. above sea-level.
BUINAKI, a town of Russia in Europe, in Georgia, in the prov. of Daghestan, 45 m. NNE of Derbent.
BULUN, a village of Siberia, on the l. bank of the Lena, in N lat. 70° 45'.

BURIASCO, a village of Piedmont, cap. of a mandemento in the prov. and 4 m. E of Pignerol, on the Lemma. BURIATS, BURAE'TS, or BURIATES, one of the three great families into which the Mongols are divided. They are chiefly located around the Baikal lake, and in the S part of the Russian gov. of Irkutsk. They are closely allied to the natives of the N provinces of China in language and customs. Their features exhibit the projecting cheek-bones and small oblique elongated eye of the Mongols; their hair is jet black, and plaited into a long queue; their complexion brown; and their frames are robust and compact. They live in conical huts, which they protect from heat and cold by covering with leather. Their religion is partly Lamaism and partly Shamanism; the latter is chiefly professed among those families who subsist by the chase, and whose houses are in the less accessible districts. The Russians have translated the Greek catechism into the B. language. A considerable number support themselves by the produce of their flocks, and by practising several mechanical arts. Their numbers have been variously estimated at from 100,000 to 300,000.

txt: BYCHOK, a town of Russia in Europe, in the gov. of Voronets, district of Pavlovsk, and 11 m. NW of Bogoutchar.
BYKHOV (Novo), a town of Russia, in the gov. of Moghilev, on the r. bank of the Dnieper, 15 m. S by E of Bykhov-Staroi.

BYKHOV-STAROI, a town of Russia, cap. of a district in the gov. and 30 m. S of Moghilev, on the r. bank of the Dnieper. Pop. 3,900. It is surrounded by an earthen rampart and ditch, and defended by two large towers over the gates. It contains 2 Russian and 2 United Greek churches, a synagogue, several convents, and a castle which formerly belonged to the Sapieha family. This town was built by the hetman of Lithuania, Sapieha, in the reign of Sigismond.
BYSTRITSA, a town of Russia in Europe, in the gov. and 25 m. ENE of Vilna, on the l. bank of the Viliya.

YAMSK, or Jamsk (Bay of), or Gouba-Jamskaia, a bay of Russia in Asia, formed by the sea of Okhotsk, on the coast of the district of that name, and to the SW of the bay of Ijighinsk, in N lat. 58° 50', and E long. 174° 20'. It is about 54 m. in length from E to W, and 24 m. in width from N to S. To the N of its entrance is Cape Olemi, and at the W extremity, near the town of Jamsk, it receives the Yama. This bay forms a commodious port, but the entrance is rendered dangerous by sand banks and sunken rocks.

KARAJINSK, or KARAJI, an island off the E coast of Kamtchatka, between the parallels of 59° 15' and 50° 28'. It is nearly 60 m. in length from NNE to SSW, and from 6 to 12 m. broad. In the summer-months it is visited by the inhabitants of the ostrogs or hamlets on the adjacent main for the purpose of hunting black and red foxes, reindeer, and game.—The river Kuraja, which descends from the Palau ridge, flows in a SSE course into the bay of K. on the main, opposite Cape Semenov on the W coast of this island.

PATIENCE, or TERPENICA (BAY), an indentation of the E coast of the island of Saghalien, opening to the S, and extending from Cape Soimonov on the W, to Cape Patience on the E, a distance of about 90 m. Cape Patience is in N lat. 48° 52', E long. 144° 30'.

SOTSHA, a river of Circassia, which falls into the Black sea, in N lat. 43° 36′, 70 m. direct distance NW of Sukhum-Kaleh. It is a fine river, holding a SSW course of about 34 m. through a beautiful valley bounded by steep well-wooded hills. Near its mouth, on a hill commanding the sea, the Russians have built a fort called Navaginskoi, which they blew up when compelled to retire from it in the summer of 1854.—A little to the SE is Cape Sotsha Bitsh, bearing 8 m. E 43° S of Cape Shubshe or Jubja.
CARADRINA, the river Drin or Drino in Rumelia. CARALITANUM PROMONTORIUM, CAGLIARI in Sardinia. CARAMBICE, Nova Zemblaia.
CARAMBUCIS, or Onius, the river OB or OBI in Asiatic Russia. CARANCEBÆ, CARANSEBES in Hungary.

CASANA, or Casanum, Kazan in Russia. CASANDRIA, CADSAND in the Dutch prov. of Zeeland. CASANUM AD ADDUAM, Casano on the Adda in Lombardy. CASCALE, Cascaos in Estremadura. CASCHOVIA, CASSOVIA, or BORMANUM, CASCHAU in Hungary.

CHUDLEIGH, a village of Russia, in the gov. of Livonia, on the W shore of Lake Peipus, 24 m. S of Neinal. The lake is here bounded by steep cliffs of a yellowish limestone rock. On the r. bank of a rapid stream, which here falls into the lake, is the castle of C., "built by and named," says Erman, "after one of a body of emigrants from Scotland, some of whose descendants still possess estates round Yeva."

CATCHINS, or CATCHINES, a Tartar tribe of Asiatic Russia, in the gov. of Tomsk, on the banks of the Jenesei. They amount to about 6,000; and are divided into 6 small hordes. They are Shamans in religion.

CAU'CASUS, an extensive mountain-system extending, like an immense wall, across the isthmus between the Black sea and the Caspian, or from the mouth of the Kuban in 44° 50' N lat. and 37° 10' E long., on the NW, to Cape Apcheron on the Caspian, in 40° 21' N lat. and 49° 40' E long., on the SE. Although the isthmus of the C. forms a kind of connecting link betwixt Europe and Western Asia, and the C. mountain-system has no immediate connexion with any of the other great mountainsystems of Europe or of Asia, yet it is now at least common to regard the C. mountains as an Asiatic system. What are called the Caucasian districts are bounded on the N by the Kuban and the Terek, into the steppes of which the mountains gradually sink; and on the S by the Black sea, the Rioni, and the Kur. The perimeter of this district presents, in general outline, the figure of an obliqueangled parallelogram, having its largest or inland sides inclined towards the SW .- The C. chain offers thirteen principal basins to the notice of the physical geographer. Of these, 7 belong to the N, and 6 to the S side. CAUCASIÆ PORTÆ, or IBERIÆ PORTÆ, the pass of VLADI-KAUKAS in the Caucasus.

CHABRAN, a town of Russia in Europe, in Daghestan, khanat and 32 m. ESE of Kouba, and 72 m. SE of Derbend, on a river of the same name which flows into the Caspian. It was founded by Nadirshah, and is rapidly falling into decay. It gives its name to a district which towards the S is extremely sterile, and which is inhabited by Persian refugees.
CHADOVO, a town of Russia in Europe, in the gov. and 100 m. NW of Vilna, district and 16 m. WNW of Poneviej.

CHADRINSK, or Shadrinsk, a town of Asiatic Russia, cap. of a district of the same name, in the gov. and 300 m. SE of Perm, on the l. bank of the Iset. Pop. 1,800. It is enclosed with palisades, contains 3 churches, and has several manufactories of soap, and tanneries. The district contains a pop. of 84,772, consisting of Bashkirs, Tartars, and Cossacks. It comprises several lakes, of which the principal is that of Maïan. The soil is generally fertile.

CHAISKOE, a lake of Russia in Europe, in the gov. of Archangel, district and 30 m. SW of Pineg. It is about 30 m. in length, and 6 in breadth.
CHAKANOVA, a town of Russia in Europe, in the gov. of Vilna, district and 16 m. NNW of Chavli.
CHAMOVO, a town of Russia in Europe, in the gov. and 45 m. NE of Moghilev, district and 17 m. NW of Mstislavl.
CHANDAGA, a river of Asiatic Russia, an affluent of the Aldan, which it joins on the r. bank, in about 136° 10' E long.

txt: CHANIA, a river of Russia in Europe, in the gov. of Kalouga, district of Medynsk. It takes its rise on the confines of the gov. of Smolensk; runs SE; and, after a course of 45 m., falls into the Oka. It has several paper-mills on its banks.
CHAOUKIANY, a town of Russia in Europe, in the gov. of Vilna, district and 22 m. SW of Chavli, near the r. bank of the Vindava.
CHARAGOLSK, a town and fort of Russia in Asia, in the gov. and 220 m. SE of Irkoutsk, near the Chinese frontier.

CHAT, a river of Russia, in the gov. of Toula, which rises near the sources of the Don, in two headstreams, and flows in a NW course to the Oripa, which it joins on the l. bank, 9 m. ESE of Toula. By the Ivanoskoi canal, it is united with the Don.
CHATAVA, a town of Russia in Europe, in the gov. of Podolia, district and 7 m. N of Kamienetz.
CHE'RECHOV, a town of Russia in Europe, in the gov. and 80 m. SSE of Grodno, district and 9 m. ESE of Proujani.
CHEIBAKPOL, a town of Russia in Europe, in the gov. and 37 m. E of Grodno, district and 27 m. SW of Lida.

CHEKSNA, a river of Russia, in the gov. of Novgorod, which, issuing from the SE side of Lake Bielo, flows in a winding but prevailingly S course to the Volga, which it joins a little above Mologa in the gov. of Jaroslav, after a course of about 240 m. Its principal affluents are the Souda, the Ouloma, the Slavenka, the Soukhona, the Pidma, the Sogoja, and the Oukhra. CHE-KYANG, CHE-KIANG, or TCHE-KIANG, a maritime province of China, lying between the parallels of 27° and 31° N lat., and, exclusive of its islands, the meridians of 118° and 121°. It is bounded on the N by the prov. of Kiang-su; on the E by the Eastern sea; on the S by the prov. of Fo-kien; and on the W by the prov. of Kiang-su and the Nganhoei or Ngan-hwai district of the prov. of Kyang-nan. Gutzlaff estimates its area at 39,150 sq. m.; and its pop. at 26,256,784. The surface of the country in the interior is generally hilly, with a reddish sandy surface; on the coast it is level, and the soil clayey. The whole is under high cultivation. Silk and tea are the staple articles of produce. The coasts are thickly studded with islands, among which the Chusan group is the most conspicuous. The rivers are numerous.
